title: Investing in All of America Act of 2025
official_summary:
Investing in All of America Act of 2025

This act modifies the limit on the amount of financing available to a Small Business Investment Company (SBIC) from the Small Business Administration (SBA). It also expands the definition of private capital with respect to SBICs.

Specifically, the act reduces the maximum outstanding financing available to an SBIC from 300% to 200% of the SBIC's private capital. The act increases from $350 million to $475 million the maximum financing available to two or more commonly controlled SBICs that make quarterly or semiannual interest payments.

The act also expands the amounts that may be excluded from the calculation of the financing limit to include the amounts an SBIC invests in (1) rural areas, (2) certain technology categories, or (3) small manufacturers. The act revises the cap on such excluded amounts to the lesser of $125 million or the aggregate of 50% of the private capital of the SBIC.

Additionally, the act expands what is considered the private capital of an SBIC to include funds obtained from the business revenue of additional government-sponsored corporations and funds invested by the trust or endowment of a college or university.

summary.headline: Law changes how much federal financing Small Business Investment Companies can get and what counts as their private money.
summary.what_it_does: Small Business Investment Companies (SBICs) are private investment funds that get financing backed by the Small Business Administration to invest in small businesses. This law lowers the usual cap on that financing from 300% to 200% of an SBIC's private money, but raises the cap for groups of SBICs under common control that make quarterly or twice-yearly interest payments from $350 million to $475 million. Money SBICs invest in rural areas, certain technology fields, or small manufacturers can be left out when figuring the cap, up to the lesser of $125 million or 50% of the SBIC's private capital. It also lets SBICs count money from college or university trusts and endowments, and from certain additional government-sponsored corporations, as private capital.

who_it_affects.how: They face a lower standard financing cap but higher limits for commonly controlled groups, plus new exclusions for certain kinds of investments.

who_it_affects.group: Small businesses in rural areas, certain technology fields, and small manufacturers
who_it_affects.how: SBICs that invest in them can leave those amounts out when figuring their financing limit.

who_it_affects.group: Colleges and universities with trusts or endowments
who_it_affects.how: Money their trusts or endowments invest in SBICs now counts as the SBIC's private capital.
It must apply the new financing limits and the broader definition of private capital when providing financing to SBICs.
